notes.key_messages: On the examination paper, there are four questions, each of which is separated into two distinct parts. The first part of the question requires shorter, more straightforward answers reflecting good knowledge of business terms and concepts whilst the second part of the question requires more developed answers containing analysis and evaluation. It remains the case that throughout this paper candidates are expected to apply their business knowledge and understanding to an unseen case study or business scenario.  To do well in this paper, candidates must make clear references, or application, to the case study which is issued at the start of the examination. Specific marks are allocated throughout the mark scheme in both parts (a) and (b) for application. In this particular case study, candidates were expected to refer to BB, which is a beauty salon. Candidates could include mention of points such as the beauty salon is in Main city, Bethany wants to expand and take on a partner as an additional manager, she has been a sole trader for 10 years, the salon has women customers of all ages, there are two qualified workers employed by Bethany, Bethany carries out the administration tasks when the salon is closed, the old equipment in the salon was purchased 10 years ago, new machines dry nails quickly, and appointments at the salon are booked by telephone.  Analytical skills are also tested throughout the examination. Candidates should try to give a full explanation of the positive and negative consequences of a business decision. This requires developed reasoning rather than simple description; listed points generally only gain level one marks whereas an explanation of a point could move the answer to level two.  Several questions on this style of paper ask candidates to make justified conclusions or recommendations. It is important to offer a decision based on balanced argument without full repetition of the previous analysis. The conclusion or recommendation should compare and make reference as to why the other alternative options were rejected as well as justifying the option which was chosen.
notes.general_comments: Candidates had been well prepared for this examination and the strong performance of many individuals is to be commended. The context of Bethany running her own beauty salon provided an accessible scenario for the majority of candidates. No question appeared to be too challenging for more than a handful of candidates. Time did not appear to be a problem. Rarely did a candidate fail to complete their answers in the one hour thirty minutes allowed. The structure of the paper allowed candidates to demonstrate their knowledge of business concepts in part (a) of each question. They were then expected to offer analysis and reasoning when answering part (b) of each question. This style of questioning has become standard practice on this particular paper and it is good to see that many candidates are developing a strong examination technique and clearly understand what is expected of them. The layout of the examination paper provides side headings to prompt candidates in their responses. This works well. As long as candidates take careful note of how many marks are awarded for each question, they should be quite clear about the extent of developed detail that is required for each answer. Many candidates showed good knowledge and understanding of the full range of the specification which was tested. Candidates could earn basic marks by defining business terms and using them confidently. Those who answered in the context of Bethany’s Beauty salon further boosted their marks. The standard of written English was excellent. Candidates made themselves fully understood and are to be congratulated on the high quality of spelling, punctuation and grammar offered in their responses. There is no penalty for the wrong spelling of words or using incorrect punctuation. However, please advise candidates that if they continue their answers on blank pages they should clearly indicate this on the question paper. The points below might be helpful in enabling candidates to achieve higher marks by using their knowledge in a more effective way.  In part (a) of each question there is a line for making a point and then a space below to explain or develop the reasoning. Candidates should think carefully about the context of the business in the case study before making their point and should ensure they do not repeat themselves in the explanation section. For example, Identify and explain two reasons why effective communication between Bethany and her employees is important. Relatively easy marks will be awarded for demonstrating knowledge of two reasons why effective communication is important to Bethany. If the explanation re-states the point in a few more words then no extra marks will be awarded. A weak explanation might follow which just states that it is to ensure instruction are understood. Instead the explanation that follows should make clear that if instructions are not understood then mistakes are likely to be made which would have an effect on the reputation of the salon. Client appointments might be booked incorrectly and so appointments are missed leading to beauticians standing around and being paid for doing nothing.  Knowledge and understanding of how to calculate profit is part of the assessment in this subject and candidates should prepare for a question that will ask them to carry out these calculations. For example, Consider the weekly forecasts in Appendix 2 for the possible additional services. Recommend which service Bethany should choose. Justify your answer using profit calculations for the two services. There are three levels of response to this answer where candidates are expected to explain and calculate the profits for each of the two options for additional services at the salon. Answers that simply offer generic statements, such as the price charged for hairdressing will be $20 higher than for sun tan beds, would only be rewarded with level 1 credit. Good answers that calculate the profits for each additional service could earn level 2 marks. Using the context of the beauty salon, a strong answer would contain analysis of the results of the profit calculations. In the final part of the answer, candidates are expected to evaluate the two additional services and to judge which would be the best one to use for this salon. This tests the candidates’ ability to synthesise and requires a clear justification as to why the other option might be less suitable and why the one they chose is more suitable.
notes.1a: The majority of candidates made a good start to the examination by correctly identifying two reasons why Bethany would want to remain small such as it would give her control over the business, gain customer loyalty and that Bethany could not afford to expand or that costs may increase. Candidates were often able to gain application marks for this question by referring to the business being a salon or that she had been a sole trader for 10 years. However, most candidates were only able to gain a maximum of two application marks because the response did not contain sufficient application for full marks.
notes.1b: Many candidates showed a good understanding of how these factors affected Bethany’s choice of partner. Some weaker responses confused the partner with either a manager or an employee. Better answers focused on using the context carefully to support their reasoning. To gain level three marks, candidates needed to go beyond repeating their level 2 comments and draw comparisons with the rejected alternatives such as knowledge of new technology might be more important than having capital to invest if the new equipment is leased. This would allow Bethany to choose the best new technology on the advice of the new partner and it could be used in the salon very quickly. This would increase revenue without a large capital outlay to buy the equipment and the partner would not need to invest a large amount of capital.
notes.2a: The majority of candidates answered this question well and discussed key areas such as the customer loyalty, local competitors and ordering the correct products to use in the salon. Candidates often gained application marks for including the fact that customers were women and other information about the business in the context. However, once again, most candidates only tended to gain two out of the four available application marks.
notes.2b: The answers to this question often scored very well. Most candidates made effective use of the insert material and earned level 2 credit by analysing the advantages and disadvantages of each of the ways to achieve good quality service at the salon. This was one of the better answered questions on the paper and even weaker responses were able to access the higher marks. Common mistakes were made in the final point where candidates didn’t understand what materials the salon would need. Some candidates gained only the first mark in level 3 for the conclusion because their explanations were too general and did not link to the impact on the business or why the other two ways were not as effective. The recommendation was best answered when there was ‘joined up’ thinking. Thus links to low price leading to higher sales but smaller profit margins and customer suspicions of low price equalling low quality.
notes.3a: Although generally well answered by the majority of candidates, this question highlighted a basic misconception of a number of candidates regarding fixed and variable costs. For example ‘Rent is a fixed cost as it probably won’t change very much’. ‘Wages go up and down as BB might not think they are working very hard’. In some cases candidates gave the correct examples for fixed and variable costs, however their explanation highlighted they didn’t have an understanding of the costs. Candidates often put wages and electricity as the wrong examples and couldn’t justify their choice.
notes.3b: This question allowed most candidates to access high marks. Many were able to work out the profit calculations correctly. However, very few candidates gained application marks as their answer focused on figures given in the appendix and nothing more. Many candidates gained high level 3 marks in the conclusion as they were able to develop the point well with good reasoning and use of the data about which additional service the business owner should adopt.
notes.4a: Many candidates answered this question well. However, a common error was to identify the customer not the employee as the central part of the answer. Candidates should be advised to read the question more than once to ensure they are answering it with the correct focus. Application marks were relatively easy to gain, but were often not achieved. Some cited examples of methods of communication – for example meetings, phone – rather than its importance.
notes.4b: This was the often the lowest scoring question on scripts. There were many generalised answers that stated ‘new technology is quicker/more efficient/more wanted by customers’. The lack of specific contextualisation when stating how technology could improve the business lost marks. The best responses suggested that SMS would enable confirmation of appointments and help to prevent loss of revenue from a missed booking. Also the customer would be able to re-arrange a booking and staff could be alerted so a replacement customer could now take their place. The case study provided plenty of material for candidates developing contextual answers to gain high marks. These marks can easily be gained but are often not achieved. Better responses included a recommendation that clearly justified why one of the ways would be more successful than the alternative two ways at having the greatest effect on the profit of the salon.
